articles.title: 1 shot, 1 key pass, 94% passing accuracy: Andrey Santos helps Brazil to 4-0 win over India
articles.summary: Manchester United midfielder Andrey Santos got some valuable minutes under his belt in Brazil’s 4-0 win over India in a friendly on Saturday, 3 April, at the...
articles.body:
Manchester United midfielder Andrey Santos got some valuable minutes under his belt in Brazil's 4-0 win over India in a friendly on Saturday, 3 April, at the Salt Lake Stadium, Kolkata. The 22-year-old has struggled for minutes since arriving at Old Trafford this summer from Chelsea.

Signed as part of succession plans for Casemiro, who left this summer, Santos saw a lot of action during pre-season. However, his game time has reduced significantly since the start of the new season due to the presence of Youri Tielemans, who also joined the Red Devils this summer.

The Belgian has started six of Manchester United's seven games so far, displaying signs of a budding partnership with Kobbie Mainoo . Meanwhile, Carlos Baleba, who was United's third midfield signing this summer, is close to full fitness, so Santos' situation is unlikely to improve.

Nevertheless, Santos was called up to the national team squad for the international break and he was included in the starting XI against India.

Carlos Ancelotti partnered Santos with Danilo Santos and Gabriel Bontempo in a three-man midfield. While the game started as an even affair, it was Brazil who took the lead as expected in the 28th minute through Estevao.

India did have their moments in the game, but it was the Selecao who doubled the lead through Pedro Guilherme at the stroke of half-time. Samuel Lino then put the game to bed in the 58th minute.

The Blue Tigers did threaten to break away on a couple of occasions later in the game but Brazil had a pretty comfortable outing. They finally made it 4-0 through Samuel Lino's second of the night in what was the last kick of the game.

Santos' performance, meanwhile, will also please Carrick ahead of what is likely to be a congested fixture list once club football resumes.

Santos had 43 touches of the ball in the game, and registered 34 passes with a 94% passing accuracy. He also managed one key pass and his one attempted cross successfully found a team-mate.

The Brazilian won three of his attempted five duels and lost possession three times. He had a relatively comfortable day in the middle of the park, registering two clearances, one interception and one tackle.

The United man, however, was dribbled past once. Santos, however, did not make much of a contribution in the final third; he did register one shot in the game, which was blocked.

The player was finally replaced by Matheus Martinelli in the 61st minute, with the game all but over.

While Santos was not overtly impressive against a relatively modest opponent, the experience will certainly benefit him. United will also be counting on the Brazilian as they prepare to play eight games in the space of a month.

articles.title: In the 1950s, immigrant tenants in Boston’s West End resisted redevelopment that levelled nearly every neighbouring brownstone; a tiny building in the North Station project area became the area’s last tenement
articles.summary: Discover the story of the last surviving tenement in Boston's West End and the resilience of immigrant tenants against urban redevelopment in the 1950s.
articles.body: Near North Station in Boston, a narrow brick walk-up stands squeezed between glass and concrete. It looks like it took a wrong turn somewhere, and in a way it did. It is what remains of a neighborhood that was cleared so completely that locals now call this one building the last tenement. It is not clear why the building at 42 Lomasney Way remained standing. Various accounts exist, including stories about tenants who refused to leave and claims that behind-the-scenes influence played a role. One documented fact is that 42 Lomasney Way remained standing while major redevelopment transformed the surrounding area. According to The West End Museum, the building was located within the North Station urban renewal project area rather than the West End project area.The West End held 23 nationalities before renewalBoston By Foot describes the old West End as a multicultural neighborhood that represented 23 nationalities before urban renewal transformed the area. In its tour description, the organization explains that urban renewal took place from the late 1950s into the 1960s, during which period over 2,500 families or 10,000 people were displaced.Boston declared the West End blighted in 1953According to The West End Museum's article The Last West Enders, the redevelopment proceeded through the use of eminent domain. All of this was done through the power of eminent domain as the city declared the neighborhood a blighted area in 1953 and began to raze the slums that housed the immigrants and their descendants. The process of razing went on for eighteen months between 1958 and 1959. There have been variations depending on where one looks as far as figures go. There was an entry in another museum about psychologist Marc Fried that gave 48 acres with 2,700 families involved, which is different from what the walking-tour group came up with.Elizabeth Blood resisted removal on Charles Street in 1960Resistance to urban renewal took many forms. One example, separate from the story of 42 Lomasney Way, involved Elizabeth Blood's eviction struggle at 379 Charles Street. By spring 1960, only 379 Charles Street remained. The occupant, Elizabeth Kearney Blood, had come from Ireland in 1918, and in May 1960 she and her two daughters resisted eviction. The women attempted to physically prevent access after the movers removed the front door from its hinges, and ultimately Blood sat herself on the hood of her car as her belongings were taken out of the house. She did succeed, however, in securing a slight victory through negotiation by the lawyer, Endicott Peabody, who later became the governor of Massachusetts, for one month of additional residency.The last tenement sat in a different project areaHowever, the very same article reports that the tenement at 42 Lomasney Way used to have more than 40 people in it. In the 1970s, its occupants were John and Rose Swietlikowski, Polish immigrants who had lived in the building with their children for roughly 50 years. The article offers several explanations for why the building remained standing. As reported in the article, the building was part of the North Station urban renewal project area, unlike the more well-known West End project area. One version suggests that the building may have been spared because of alleged Mafia connections, as its owner in 1972 was William Kazonis, an associate of New England Mafia boss Gennaro Angiulo. Later projects such as the Green Line and the Big Dig also did not remove the building.Marc Fried studied how displaced residents grievedThe best-known research on the West End's loss came from Fried, whose work the museum covers in its article Marc Fried and the Human Cost of Urban Renewal. In the West End, Fried interviewed hundreds of displaced residents in the late 1950s and worked with a team that embedded itself in neighborhood life to document pre-relocation and post-relocation effects. The study suggested that losing homes could also mean losing social ties and identity. Fried described that disruption as a form of bereavement, and later scholarship has cited the research as foundational to discussions about community displacement and root shock.Drawing on interviews conducted before and after relocation, Fried published Grieving for a Lost Home in 1963, a study that examined residents' emotional responses to displacement and demolition. Thus, he published his paper Grieving for a Lost Home in 1963.Fried described the loss as root shockAlso as noted in the article above, Fried found that such closely knit communities provided individuals with a sense of rootedness. According to Fried, destroying tightly connected communities could cause significant psychological distress. Later, psychiatrist Mindy Fullilove described similar community disruption through the concept of "root shock." One interviewee, Mrs. Borowski, compared it to uprooting a plant from its surroundings. The research suggested that people could mourn not only the loss of a person but also the loss of a place and way of life. In fact, it had an effect on how community mental health care was handled, not to mention urban renewal projects in the United States.Fried's research joined a wider body of criticismThe museum further adds that the article by Fried was included in Urban Renewal: The Record and the Controversy, a book compiled by the Joint Center for Urban Studies, a collaborative effort between Harvard and MIT. This book also contained contributions from Herbert Gans, Martin Anderson, and activist Chester Hartman. A decade later, Fried published The World of the Urban Working Class: Social Movements and Ideology (1973), drawing on years of research connected to the West End.You use AI every day. articles.title: Somalia won’t accept Israeli presence ‘under any circumstances’: President
articles.summary: In exclusive Al Jazeera interview, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud says Israel planning a naval base in Berbera.
articles.body:
Somalia will not accept Israeli presence in the country “under any circumstances” and will resist any attempts to be pulled into the Middle East’s crises, its President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud tells Al Jazeera.

Speaking in an exclusive interview, Mohamud said that Israel was planning to establish a naval base in Berbera and use the city’s airport, adding that its real aim was to get closer to the Gulf states and Iran.

Berbera is a port city on the Gulf of Aden coast in Somaliland – the self-declared republic in northwestern Somalia that Israel recognised last year, but which is claimed by Mogadishu.

Berbera faces Yemen across the water near the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait. The Iran-aligned Houthis have previously enforced a blockade on Israel-linked ships in the area.

“We will overcome the challenges posed to our country by Israeli moves,” Mohamud said in his wide-ranging interview.

He added that the Israeli plans fall under the “ Greater Israel ” project – referring to a term for various proposals, often rooted in biblical interpretations, for Israeli control over territory beyond its current borders. Some versions extend from the Nile to the Euphrates.

Israel has not adopted it as official policy, but Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in an August 2025 interview that he felt connected to the vision, prompting condemnation from Arab governments.

The Somali president described Israel as a “destabilising force” that does not abide by international law.

He also criticised Tel Aviv’s recognition of Somaliland in December.

No country other than Israel recognises Somaliland, while the region’s own residents are completely opposed to an Israeli presence, Mohamud said.

Somaliland declared independence from Somalia in 1991 and has governed itself independently for more than three decades. But it had not secured recognition from any United Nations member state until Israel’s move.

The Somali president told Al Jazeera the United States remains his country’s strongest partner in the fight against “terrorism”, and added that al-Shabab has no presence in the major cities, leaving no possibility of the group taking control in Somalia.

Al-Shabab is a Somali armed group that emerged from the Islamic Courts Union in the mid-2000s and pledged allegiance to al-Qaeda in 2012. It has fought Somalia’s federal government for years, holds territory in parts of southern and central Somalia, and has carried out deadly attacks, including in Mogadishu and in neighbouring Kenya.

Regarding the East Africa region, Mohamud said Somalia’s relations with neighbouring Ethiopia are good, and Mogadishu does not object to Addis Ababa gaining access to the sea through a joint agreement to use Somali ports for its economic interests.

Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea became independent in 1993 and relies largely on Djibouti’s ports for trade. In January 2024, Addis Ababa signed a memorandum of understanding with Somaliland on sea access, which Somalia condemned as a violation of its sovereignty. Somalia and Ethiopia later agreed to ease tensions.

Mohamud also accused Yemen’s Houthis of “destabilising the region” and disrupting navigation in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

His comments come as the group attempts to build on its lightning offensive that captured the country’s Red Sea coast last month.

Thus far, Yemeni government forces have been able to hold their positions on the front lines and even claimed to have inflicted heavy losses against the Houthis.

The Houthis have also intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia, but the kingdom’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) has promised not to compromise on its security, saying the Yemeni rebels chose “chaos and destruction, threatening the Yemeni people and the region”.

The full interview with President Mohamud will be broadcast on Al Jazeera Arabic on Sunday.

articles.title: In 2013, Indianapolis spent $14 million turning a $1 abandoned baseball stadium into 138 apartments, keeping the old grandstand as residents’ view
articles.summary: Discover how Indianapolis turned the abandoned Bush Stadium into Stadium Lofts with 138 apartments while preserving its historic charm. A $14 million transformation that revitalized a piece of sports history.
articles.body: Residents moved into Stadium Lofts in Indianapolis in 2013, which used to be a baseball stadium back in the day. The old Bush Stadium had been converted into 138 apartments, and much of the original structure was retained and the baseball field was still visible from the homes. The developers had acquired the abandoned stadium for just $1 and spent about $14 million on the conversion.Bush Stadium opened in 1931, became home to the Indianapolis Indians and later hosted baseball during the 1987 Pan American Games. The stadium also appeared as a stand-in for Chicago's Comiskey Park in the 1988 film Eight Men Out. After the Indians moved downtown to Victory Field in 1996, the old ballpark went through less conventional uses, which included a short-lived dirt-track racing operation and a period when the site was used to store vehicles from the federal Cash for Clunkers program.Bush Stadium had been sitting without a clear long-term purpose by the time Core Redevelopment took on the property, with the company choosing to preserve the structure rather than replacing it with a conventional apartment building. The Downtown Indianapolis development record describes Stadium Lofts as a renovation of the former stadium and lists 138 housing units and $5.3 million in public funding.Apartments were built inside the old ballparkThe conversion began in 2011 and the finished development contained studios, one-bedroom apartments and two-bedroom units, with the existing stadium forming part of the residential complex. Geralyn Strecker was the first resident to sign a lease, with her living room being positioned behind home plate, which meant that the former baseball field was still part of her view after the stadium had become her home. When Stadium Lofts opened on July 27, 2013, all 138 units had been leased.Original features were incorporated into the redevelopment, while the relationship between the apartments and the old field remained visible. The idea was to retain enough of the old building for residents to see what had been there before, which made the project different from a typical historic renovation.The $1 purchase was only the beginningThe stadium itself changed hands for $1, while the redevelopment cost roughly $14 million. Indianapolis Business Journal reported that the project combined public and private financing, which included a $5 million city contribution, while the city’s current development record lists $5.3 million in public dollars.The developers also had to convince people that apartments in an old ballpark could work, since the neighborhood around the stadium had not yet become the residential and technology district that later development would bring. At the time, the project was therefore a bet on both the building and the surrounding area. Core planned another 144 apartments beside the former ballpark, known as Stadium Flats. Construction on that phase began in October 2013, and expanded the residential redevelopment beyond the apartments inside the old stadium.People had come to Bush Stadium to watch games for decades, but after the redevelopment, residents could still look across and view the same former playing area from their homes. Stadium Lofts opened in 2013 with 138 apartments, and turned a stadium that had spent years without a clear future into housing. The $1 acquisition price became the memorable part of the story, but the more consequential decision was that instead of demolishing the old ballpark, the developers made its structure part of the homes built inside it.You use AI every day. articles.title: Zach Bryan wears ‘Free Palestine’ shirt at Gillette Stadium concert, weeks after Ed Sheeran tour uproar
articles.summary: Country singer Zach Bryan wore a “Free Palestine” T-shirt during his concert at Gillette Stadium near Boston on Friday night, weeks after stadium’s owner Robert Kraft was accused of pressuring Ed Sheeran to drop his opening act over pro-Palestinian remarks.
articles.body: Country singer Zach Bryan wore a “Free Palestine” T-shirt during his concert at Gillette Stadium near Boston on Friday night, weeks after stadium’s owner Robert Kraft was accused of pressuring Ed Sheeran to drop his opening act over pro-Palestinian remarks. Videos across social media showed Bryan, 30, wearing a black cutoff T-shirt with “Free Palestine” in white letters during his tour stop at the stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. Kraft, who owns the New England Patriots, is a staunch supporter of Israel. Last month, rapper Macklemore said he was removed from Sheeran’s tour at Kraft’s behest after he spoke out in support of Palestinians at the tour’s shows in New Jersey. Kraft did not immediately return a request for comment. He has said he did not want to stifle support for Palestinians but to ensure a “welcoming environment” at Gillette Stadium for Sheeran’s tour. Sheeran’s other opening acts — Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham, Finneas and his house band, Beoga — withdrew from the tour in protest after Macklemore’s removal. Sheeran apologized for how he handled the matter in his first show since news broke of Macklemore’s removal. “I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician,” Sheeran said, “but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet.” Last week, Macklemore announced a Free Palestine Tour for this fall. Gillette Stadium will not be one of its stops. The Israeli-Palestinian conflict has been a flashpoint in pop culture for decades. Israel’s war in Gaza has killed more than 70,000 people there, according to local health authorities. It followed the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel, in which more than 1,200 people were killed. Differences over the war have permeated everything from local political contests to the Costume Institute exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Bryan is best known for his songs “Something in the Orange,” “I Remember Everything” featuring Kacey Musgraves and “Pink Skies.” The Grammy-winning artist served in the U.S. Navy for several years while continuing to write and record music.

articles.title: In 1979, Sally Quinn and Ben Bradlee paid $220,000 for New York's decaying Grey Gardens and restored it; 38 years later, the 6,000-sq-ft East Hampton estate sold for $15.5 million
articles.summary: In 1979, Washington Post journalist Sally Quinn and executive editor Ben Bradlee bought the infamous Grey Gardens estate in East Hampton for $220,000,
articles.body: In 1979, Washington Post journalist Sally Quinn and executive editor Ben Bradlee bought the infamous Grey Gardens estate in East Hampton for $220,000, rescuing a decaying 1897 mansion that had become a symbol of bohemian decline. After restoring the 6,000-square-foot home and using it as a summer residence for decades, the property changed hands again in late 2017, selling for $15.5 million to an undisclosed buyer. The sale, first reported by The Real Deal, marked the latest chapter in the storied history of a house made famous by a 1975 documentary and later by an HBO film and Broadway musical.From Gilded Age estate to cinematic iconGrey Gardens was built in 1897 on Georgica Pond in East Hampton, a 12-room mansion set on 1.7 acres of land. The property became widely known not for its architecture but for its most famous residents, Edith Bouvier Beale and her daughter Edith Beale, known as Big Edie and Little Edie. The two women, relatives of Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, lived in increasingly impoverished and eccentric conditions as the house fell into disrepair. The estate gained cultural importance after filmmakers Albert and David Maysles released a documentary in 1975 called Gray Gardens, which captured the Beales’ unusual lifestyle amid the overgrown gardens and crumbling interiors. The film turned it into a cultural landmark and inspired later adaptations, including an HBO special and a Broadway musical. By the time Quinn and Bradlee bought the property in 1979, it had become a symbol of both Gilded Age grandeur and countercultural decay, the report said.A rescue mission by two media powerhouses Sally Quinn and Ben Bradlee were already prominent figures in American journalism when they bought Gray Gardens. Under the leadership of Bradlee, who led The Washington Post during the Watergate years, and Quinn, a prominent writer and television personality, the possibilities in the long-neglected estate were seen. They began an extensive repair and restoration project, bringing the mansion back to a state of its original elegance, yet keeping its quirky personality intact.Gray Gardens was the couple's summer home for more than three decades. The property became a retreat from Washington's political intensity, a place where they could host friends and enjoy the Hamptons' coastal setting. Bradlee died in 2014, and Quinn continued to maintain the home until the decision to sell. Their stewardship transformed Grey Gardens from a notorious ruin into a restored estate with a renewed sense of dignity, reported The Real Deal.The road to a $15.5 million saleWhen Grey Gardens returned to the market, it carried both historical cachet and a premium price tag. The property was listed in early 2017 for $20 million, reflecting its fame, location on Georgica Pond, and the extensive work that had gone into its restoration. By December, the estate sold for $15.5 million, a $4.5 million discount from the asking price, according to listing agent Michael Schultz of The Corcoran Group.The buyer remained undisclosed, adding to the mystique of a property that has always attracted public curiosity. The sale price placed Grey Gardens among the most notable Hamptons transactions of the year, underscoring the enduring appeal of estates with deep cultural histories. For Quinn, the sale closed a chapter that began nearly 40 years earlier when she and Bradlee took a chance on a crumbling mansion.Why Grey Gardens remains unique in the HamptonsThe Hamptons real estate market is filled with grand estates, but few properties carry the same blend of architectural history, celebrity connection, and pop culture resonance as Grey Gardens. Its history runs from the Gilded Age to the counterculture 1970s and into the age of high-profile media personalities. Each chapter in that story added another layer of meaning to what it was, more than a big house on prime land.The mansion is 6,000 square feet, on 1.7 acres on Georgica Pond, a prized spot in East Hampton. Quinn and Bradlee’s restoration work allowed the house to serve as a contemporary residence while preserving the details that made it unique. For buyers, the attraction is not only in the physical attributes but also in the opportunity to own a piece of cultural history.A reflection of Hamptons market dynamicsThe sale of Grey Gardens took place against a backdrop of shifting dynamics in the Hamptons luxury market. In 2017, Sagaponack, long ranked as the nation's most expensive zip code, fell to 15th place as more sales occurred at lower price points. Gray Gardens made it onto the list of the top ten most expensive zip codes with median sales prices over $3 million, joining Water Mill and Wainscott. “Properties with a storied past and a prime location are still drawing interest, even in a cooling market. Gray Gardens has proven that cultural relevance can carry weight even as broader market trends change. The $15.5 million sale price, though down from the original asking price, still delivered a handsome return on the $220,000 Quinn and Bradlee spent in 1979.From decay to preservation and back againEssentially, the Gray Gardens story is one of transformation. It began as a crumbling mansion occupied by eccentric relatives of a former first lady, and has been restored into an estate under the guidance of two journalism icons. The property’s trajectory reflects larger themes of preservation, reinvention, and the lasting power of place.The sale validated the vision Sally Quinn and Bradlee brought to the property nearly four decades ago, but it also marked the end of an era. For the new owners, Gray Gardens offers a rare combination of privacy, prestige and historical depth. One of East Hampton’s most talked about estates, it remains a landmark not only on Georgica Pond but in the cultural imagination of the Hamptons and beyond.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Watch: Netanyahu invites PM Modi, pilot Smit Machchhar to Israel I-Day event
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has invited Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar to light a flame at Israel's Independence Day event, calling him
articles.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has invited Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar to light a flame at Israel's Independence Day event, calling him a "hero" of Israel, India and the entire world for foiling an alleged attempt to crash an Israel-bound flydubai flight.Netanyahu spoke to the 38-year-old pilot on Saturday while Machchhar was undergoing treatment at a hospital in the UAE. During the emotional conversation, Machchhar recounted how he was attacked by his co-pilot inside the cockpit and revealed new details about the incident."It's our highest honour that we give on our Independence Day. It's usually reserved for Israeli citizens, but I think here in this case, all the citizens of Israel will embrace you. They do now, and they will then too. So we hope to see you very soon in Israel," Netanyahu told Machchhar.The Israeli Prime Minister's office later said on X, "You are a hero for Israel, India, and the entire world. I invite Prime Minister Narendra Modi and you to light a flame on Israeli Independence Day.""During the emotional conversation that took place this evening, the Prime Minister asked Captain Machchhar how it all started, and Machchhar revealed new details about the terrifying moments in the cockpit," the post said.Machchhar told Netanyahu that the co-pilot had wanted to pray before the attack. He said he looked towards the front of the cockpit out of respect while the co-pilot prayed."...while he was praying, out of respect, I was just looking at the front and not at the back, and suddenly, after, I would say about four-five minutes, there was a big blow to the back of my head."My first thought was that there was catastrophic damage to the aircraft and something was not right. But then after that, the blows kept coming one after the other, and that's when I realised that it's not the aircraft, it's the other guy who was in the cockpit with me," Machchhar said.Netanyahu praised the pilot for his actions during the incident."You saved so many souls. I think you saved something bigger. You saved the spirit of the world...It's something that is being justly hailed around the world. You're a hero of Israel. You're a hero of India. You're a hero of the entire world," Netanyahu told Machchhar."You know, I guess it's a twist of fate, and a twist of faith, and what you did is remarkable. I heard, of course, from the Israeli passengers what transpired after that, and you're a great hero, and you were accompanied by heroes, and you saved the day," he said.Netanyahu also told Machchhar he was "amazed at his courage" and "at your coolness of judgment under impossible conditions."The incident took place on Wednesday aboard flydubai flight FZ1073, which was carrying 174 passengers to Israel. Machchhar was allegedly attacked by his co-pilot with a crash axe, an emergency tool kept inside the cockpit.The aircraft transmitted emergency signals and made a rapid descent of more than 17,000 feet, from 34,000 feet. It eventually made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. The descent was so extreme that part of the aircraft's rudder was reportedly torn away.The co-pilot has been identified as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, according to a Wall Street Journal report citing people familiar with the matter.Machchhar received initial treatment in Tabuk before being shifted to Abu Dhabi for continued medical care.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
